claim: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma is currently the third leading cause of cancer-related deaths in the United States with a 5-y survival rate of 12%
source: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDA) is currently the third leading cause of cancer-related deaths in the United States with a 5-y survival rate of 12% (Siegel et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim cites Siegel et al., 2023 as the source for the statistic about PDA being the third leading cause of cancer-related deaths and having a 12% 5-year survival rate.

claim: The hallmark mutation in PDA is found in the KRAS gene, most commonly KRASG12D
source: The hallmark mutation in PDA is found in the KRAS gene, most commonly KRASG12D (Hezel et al., 2006; Hingorani et al., 2003; Hingorani et al., 2005; Schneider and Schmid, 2003)
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations (Hezel et al., 2006; Hingorani et al., 2003; Hingorani et al., 2005; Schneider and Schmid, 2003) that establish KRASG12D as the most common mutation in PDA.

claim: Disease progression in PDA is accelerated by loss of tumor suppressor genes, including TP53, SMAD4, and INK4A
source: whereas disease progression is accelerated by loss of tumor suppressor genes, including TP53, SMAD4, and INK4A (Hezel et al., 2006; Maitra and Hruban, 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hezel et al., 2006 and Maitra and Hruban, 2008, which document the role of tumor suppressor gene loss in PDA progression.

claim: Standard of care for PDA is a combination of systemic chemotherapy that includes FOLFIRINOX or gemcitabine plus nab-paclitaxel
source: Standard of care for PDA is a combination of systemic chemotherapy that includes FOLFIRINOX or gemcitabine plus nab-paclitaxel (Mizrahi et al., 2020)
evidence: The claim cites Mizrahi et al., 2020 as the source for the standard of care treatment regimens for PDA.

claim: FOLFIRINOX or gemcitabine plus nab-paclitaxel provides limited improvement in patient survival
source: Standard of care for PDA is a combination of systemic chemotherapy that includes FOLFIRINOX or gemcitabine plus nab-paclitaxel (Mizrahi et al., 2020), which provides limited improvement in patient survival.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Mizrahi et al., 2020 and represents established knowledge about the limited efficacy of current standard treatments.

claim: Oncogenic KRAS proteins were long thought to be 'undruggable'
source: Oncogenic KRAS proteins were long thought to be 'undruggable' (Gysin et al., 2011; Liu et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Gysin et al., 2011 and Liu et al., 2019, which document the historical view of KRAS as an undruggable target.

claim: New approaches to drug discovery have led to the development of KRASG12C inhibitors
source: Recently, new approaches to drug discovery have led to the development of KRASG12C inhibitors (Canon et al., 2019; Fell et al., 2020)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Canon et al., 2019 and Fell et al., 2020, which describe the development of KRASG12C inhibitors.

claim: KRASG12C is a common mutation in non-small cell lung cancer
source: KRASG12C inhibitors (Canon et al., 2019; Fell et al., 2020), a common mutation in non-small cell lung cancer (Prior et al., 2012)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Prior et al., 2012, which documents the prevalence of KRASG12C mutations in non-small cell lung cancer.

claim: Initial clinical data for KRASG12C inhibitors show dramatic responses but also cases of primary or secondary resistance
source: initial clinical data show not only dramatic responses but also cases of primary or secondary resistance (Awad et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Awad et al., 2021, which reports clinical outcomes of KRASG12C inhibitors.

claim: The applicability of G12C inhibitors is limited in PDA, which rarely presents with this specific allele
source: While the applicability of G12C inhibitors is limited in PDA, which is rarely present with this specific allele (Witkiewicz et al., 2015)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Witkiewicz et al., 2015, which documents the rarity of KRASG12C mutations in PDA.

claim: New KRASG12D inhibitors have recently been described and are entering the clinic
source: new KRASG12D inhibitors have recently been described and are entering the clinic (Hallin et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hallin et al., 2022 and Wang et al., 2022, which describe the development of KRASG12D inhibitors.

claim: Resistance to KRAS G12D inhibitors is expected to arise based on observations in lung cancer and predictions from mouse models
source: Based on the observations in lung cancer (Awad et al., 2021; Zhao et al., 2021) and on predictions based on mouse models that allow genetic inactivation of oncogenic KRAS (Collins et al., 2012; Ying et al., 2012), it is to be expected that resistance to KRAS G12D inhibitors will similarly arise
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations documenting resistance in lung cancer and mouse models, and represents an inference about future resistance patterns.

claim: Activation of anti-tumor immune responses remains our best hope for long-term tumor control
source: activation of anti-tumor immune responses remains our best hope for long-term tumor control.
evidence: This represents a speculative statement about future therapeutic strategies based on the expected development of resistance to targeted therapies.

claim: Immune checkpoint inhibitors are effective in other cancers but this benefit has not translated to PDA
source: Although immune checkpoint inhibitors are effective in other cancers, this benefit has not translated to PDA (Brahmer et al., 2012; Royal et al., 2010)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Brahmer et al., 2012 and Royal et al., 2010, which document the lack of efficacy of immune checkpoint inhibitors in PDA.

claim: The lack of efficacy of immune checkpoint inhibitors in PDA is due to the severely immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment
source: this benefit has not translated to PDA (Brahmer et al., 2012; Royal et al., 2010) due to the severely immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME) that characterizes this disease (Morrison et al., 2018; Vonderheide and Bayne, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Morrison et al., 2018 and Vonderheide and Bayne, 2013, which characterize the immunosuppressive TME in PDA.

claim: Approaches combining immune checkpoints and myeloid cell targeting might be more promising based on preclinical studies
source: Approaches combining immune checkpoints and myeloid cell targeting might be more promising, based on preclinical studies (DeNardo et al., 2021; Gulhati et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to preclinical studies (DeNardo et al., 2021; Gulhati et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2021) and represents a speculative statement about future therapeutic approaches.

claim: The pancreatic TME includes cancer-associated fibroblasts and a heterogenous population of immune cells, the majority of which is myeloid cells
source: The pancreatic TME includes cancer-associated fibroblasts and a heterogenous population of immune cells, the majority of which is myeloid cells (Gabrilovich and Nagaraj, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Gabrilovich and Nagaraj, 2009, which characterizes the cellular composition of the pancreatic TME.

claim: Myeloid cells in the pancreatic TME include tumor-associated macrophages, immature myeloid cells (myeloid-derived suppressor cells), and granulocytes such as neutrophils
source: These myeloid cells include tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs), immature myeloid cells, also referred to as myeloid-derived suppressor cells, and granulocytes, such as neutrophils (Gabrilovich et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Gabrilovich et al., 2012, which describes the types of myeloid cells present in the TME.

claim: CD8+ T cells are rare in the pancreatic TME, although their prevalence is heterogeneous in different patients
source: In contrast, CD8+ T cells are rare in the pancreatic TME, although their prevalence is heterogeneous in different patients (Stromnes et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Stromnes et al., 2017, which documents the rarity and heterogeneity of CD8+ T cells in PDA.

claim: Single-cell RNA sequencing analysis revealed that most CD8+ T cells infiltrating PDA have an exhausted phenotype
source: Single-cell RNA sequencing (sc-RNA-seq) analysis revealed that most CD8+ T cells infiltrating PDA have an exhausted phenotype (Steele et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Steele et al., 2020, which used sc-RNA-seq to characterize CD8+ T cell phenotypes in PDA.

claim: Analysis of long-term survivors revealed persistence of tumor-specific memory CD8+ T cells, indicating that when an anti-tumor immune response does occur, it leads to effective tumor control
source: Of note, analysis of long-term survivors revealed persistence of tumor-specific memory CD8+ T cells, indicating that when an anti-tumor immune response does occur, it leads to effective tumor control (Balachandran et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Balachandran et al., 2017, which analyzed immune responses in long-term PDA survivors.

claim: Evidence of loss of antigens over time due to immunoediting has been described in pancreatic cancer
source: Conversely, evidence of loss of antigens over time due to immunoediting has also been described (Łuksza et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Łuksza et al., 2022, which documented immunoediting in pancreatic cancer.

claim: Myeloid cell depletion in mouse models of pancreatic cancer led to activation of anti-tumor T cell responses
source: Furthermore, myeloid cell depletion in mouse models of pancreatic cancer led to activation of anti-tumor T cell responses (Mitchem et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2017a)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Mitchem et al., 2013 and Zhang et al., 2017a, which demonstrated the effect of myeloid cell depletion in mouse models.

claim: Clinical efficacy of myeloid cell targeting in pancreatic cancer has been low
source: yet, clinical efficacy has been low, and more effective approaches are needed.
evidence: The claim represents established knowledge about the limited clinical success of myeloid cell targeting strategies.

claim: Myeloid cells infiltrating the neoplastic pancreas and those in PDA express high levels of Arginase 1
source: Myeloid cells infiltrating the neoplastic pancreas, and ultimately those in PDA, express high levels of Arginase 1 (Arg1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the authors' previous work and is a key observation that motivates the current study.

claim: ARG1 is one of the enzymes that metabolize arginine, and it is prevalently located in the cytoplasm
source: ARG1 is one of the enzymes that metabolize arginine, and it is prevalently located in the cytoplasm, while the ARG2 isoform is prevalently mitochondrial (Bronte and Zanovello, 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Bronte and Zanovello, 2005, which describes the subcellular localization of arginase isoforms.

claim: The ARG2 isoform is prevalently mitochondrial
source: ARG1 is one of the enzymes that metabolize arginine, and it is prevalently located in the cytoplasm, while the ARG2 isoform is prevalently mitochondrial (Bronte and Zanovello, 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Bronte and Zanovello, 2005, which describes the subcellular localization of arginase isoforms.

claim: Arg1 expression in myeloid cells is driven by oncogenic Kras expression/signaling in epithelial cells, starting during early stages of carcinogenesis
source: Indeed, we previously showed that Arg1 expression in myeloid cells is driven by oncogenic Kras expression/signaling in epithelial cells, starting during early stages of carcinogenesis (Velez-Delgado et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2017b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to the authors' previous work (Velez-Delgado et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2017b).

claim: ARG1 is widely appreciated as a marker of alternatively polarized macrophages
source: Beyond our work, ARG1 is widely appreciated as a marker of alternatively polarized macrophages.
evidence: This represents established knowledge in the field about ARG1 as a macrophage polarization marker.

claim: An increase in tumor myeloid Arg1 expression has been reported in renal cell carcinoma
source: An increase in tumor myeloid Arg1 expression has been reported in other cancers, including renal cell carcinoma (Rodriguez et al., 2009)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Rodriguez et al., 2009, which documented Arg1 expression in renal cell carcinoma.

claim: An increase in tumor myeloid Arg1 expression has been reported in breast cancer
source: An increase in tumor myeloid Arg1 expression has been reported in other cancers, including renal cell carcinoma (Rodriguez et al., 2009), breast (Polat et al., 2003; Singh et al., 2000)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Polat et al., 2003 and Singh et al., 2000, which documented Arg1 expression in breast cancer.

claim: An increase in tumor myeloid Arg1 expression has been reported in colon cancer
source: An increase in tumor myeloid Arg1 expression has been reported in other cancers, including renal cell carcinoma (Rodriguez et al., 2009), breast (Polat et al., 2003; Singh et al., 2000), colon (Arlauckas et al., 2018)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Arlauckas et al., 2018, which documented Arg1 expression in colon cancer.

claim: An increase in tumor myeloid Arg1 expression has been reported in lung cancer
source: An increase in tumor myeloid Arg1 expression has been reported in other cancers, including renal cell carcinoma (Rodriguez et al., 2009), breast (Polat et al., 2003; Singh et al., 2000), colon (Arlauckas et al., 2018), and lung cancer (Miret et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Miret et al., 2019, which documented Arg1 expression in lung cancer.

claim: ARG1 is a metabolic enzyme that breaks down the amino acid L-arginine to urea and ornithine
source: In addition to its role as a marker of alternatively polarized macrophages, ARG1 is a metabolic enzyme that breaks down the amino acid L-arginine to urea and ornithine (Jenkinson et al., 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Jenkinson et al., 1996, which describes the enzymatic activity of ARG1.

claim: Arginine is necessary for the activation and proliferation of CD8 T cells
source: Connecting this activity to myeloid Arg1 expression, several reports detail how arginine is necessary for the activation and proliferation of CD8 T cells (Rodriguez et al., 2007; Rodriguez et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Rodriguez et al., 2007 and Rodriguez et al., 2004, which documented the requirement for arginine in CD8 T cell function.

claim: Myeloid cells may deplete arginine in the TME to dampen anti-tumor T cell activity
source: This indicates that myeloid cells may deplete arginine in the TME to dampen anti-tumor T cell activity.
evidence: This represents an inference based on the cited literature about arginine's role in T cell function and ARG1's enzymatic activity.

claim: CB-1158 is a small-molecule arginase inhibitor developed by Calithera Biosciences
source: Based on these concepts, a small-molecule arginase inhibitor, CB-1158 (INCB001158) (Calithera Biosciences, Inc, South San Francisco, CA), was developed.
evidence: This represents factual information about the development of CB-1158.

claim: CB-1158 treatment as monotherapy or in combination with anti-PD-1 checkpoint inhibitor decreased tumor growth in vivo in mice with Lewis lung carcinoma
source: CB-1158 treatment as monotherapy, or in combination with anti-PD-1 checkpoint inhibitor, decreased tumor growth in vivo in mice with Lewis lung carcinoma (Steggerda et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Steggerda et al., 2017, which demonstrated the efficacy of CB-1158 in a mouse model.

claim: CB-1158 inhibits human arginase
source: CB-1158 also inhibits human arginase, and it is being tested in a phase I clinical trial in patients with advanced or metastatic solid tumors (Pham et al., 2018; Steggerda et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Pham et al., 2018 and Steggerda et al., 2017, which describe CB-1158's activity against human arginase.

claim: CB-1158 is being tested in a phase I clinical trial in patients with advanced or metastatic solid tumors
source: CB-1158 also inhibits human arginase, and it is being tested in a phase I clinical trial in patients with advanced or metastatic solid tumors (Pham et al., 2018; Steggerda et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Pham et al., 2018 and Steggerda et al., 2017, which describe the clinical testing of CB-1158.

claim: A dual-recombinase approach was used to delete Arg1 in myeloid cell lineages via Cre-loxP technology while inducing oncogenic Kras in pancreatic epithelial cells using Flp-Frt recombination
source: Here, we used a dual-recombinase approach to delete Arg1 in myeloid cell lineages via Cre-loxP technology and at the same time induced oncogenic Kras in pancreatic epithelial cells using the orthogonal Flp-Frt recombination approach.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used in the study.

claim: Arg1 deletion in myeloid cells profoundly reshaped the TME, increased the infiltration of CD8+ T cells, and reduced malignant disease progression
source: We discovered that Arg1 deletion in myeloid cells profoundly reshaped the TME, increased the infiltration of CD8+ T cells, and reduced malignant disease progression.
evidence: This represents a summary of the experimental findings from the genetic model described in the study.

claim: Other cells in the TME, such as epithelial cells, upregulate Arg1 expression as a resistance mechanism when Arg1 is inactivated in myeloid cells
source: However, we also noticed a resistance mechanism whereby other cells in the TME, such as epithelial cells, upregulate Arg1 expression, potentially blunting the effect of its inactivation in myeloid cells.
evidence: This represents an observation from the experimental data showing compensatory Arg1 expression.

claim: Treatment of a syngeneic orthotopic model of pancreatic cancer with CB-1158 sensitized tumors to anti-PD1 immune checkpoint blockade
source: We thus employed a systemic approach, whereby we treated a syngeneic orthotopic model of pancreatic cancer with the arginase inhibitor CB-1158 and found it to sensitize PDA to anti-PD1 immune checkpoint blockade.
evidence: This represents a key finding from the pharmacological experiments in the study.

claim: ARG1 expression in CD45+ cells was prevalent in human PDA
source: We observed prevalent ARG1 expression in CD45+ cells, and occasional low expression in ECAD+ cells (Figure 1A, Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1A and quantified in Figure 1B.

claim: ARG1 expression in ECAD+ cells was occasional and low in human PDA
source: We observed prevalent ARG1 expression in CD45+ cells, and occasional low expression in ECAD+ cells (Figure 1A, Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1A and quantified in Figure 1B.

claim: Analysis of sc-RNA-seq dataset from 16 human PDA samples revealed highest expression of ARG1 in myeloid cells
source: Analysis of a previously published sc-RNA-seq dataset, which includes 16 human PDA samples (Steele et al., 2020; Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), revealed highest expression of ARG1 in myeloid cells (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of published sc-RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Minimal ARG1 expression was observed in CD4+ T cells, CD8+ T cells, epithelial cells, and fibroblasts in human PDA
source: In contrast, we observed minimal ARG1 expression in CD4+ T cells, CD8+ T cells, epithelial cells, and fibroblasts (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by sc-RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: ARG2 was expressed at high levels in endocrine cells in human PDA
source: ARG2 was expressed at high levels in endocrine cells, and at lower, but detectable levels in epithelial cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by sc-RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: ARG2 was expressed at lower, but detectable levels in epithelial cells in human PDA
source: ARG2 was expressed at high levels in endocrine cells, and at lower, but detectable levels in epithelial cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by sc-RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Myeloid cells are the main source of ARG1 in the pancreatic cancer microenvironment
source: Thus, we conclude that myeloid cells are the main source of ARG1 in the pancreatic cancer microenvironment.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the RNA ISH and sc-RNA-seq data presented in Figure 1.

claim: Infiltration of myeloid cells, specifically macrophages, in pancreatic cancer portends worse patient survival
source: Infiltration of myeloid cells, specifically macrophages, in pancreatic cancer portends worse patient survival (Sanford et al., 2013; Tsujikawa et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Sanford et al., 2013 and Tsujikawa et al., 2017.

claim: High ARG1 expression in pancreatic cancer correlated with worse survival
source: Based on a publicly available human PDA microarray data set (GSE71729) (Moffitt et al., 2015), we found that high ARG1 expression in pancreatic cancer correlated with worse survival (Figure 1E)
evidence: The claim is supported by survival analysis of the GSE71729 dataset shown in Figure 1E.

claim: High ARG1 expression correlating with worse survival suggests that ARG1 in myeloid cells may play a functional role in human PDA
source: we found that high ARG1 expression in pancreatic cancer correlated with worse survival (Figure 1E), suggesting that ARG1 in myeloid cells may play a functional role in human PDA.
evidence: This represents an inference based on the survival analysis data.

claim: The highest level of Arg1 expression in mouse pancreatic cancer was detected in macrophages
source: We detected the highest level of Arg1 expression in macrophages (Figure 1G and Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by sc-RNA-seq data from mouse models shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Arg1 expression was enriched in PDA infiltrating macrophages compared to macrophages in the normal pancreas
source: Importantly, Arg1 expression was enriched in PDA infiltrating macrophages compared to macrophages in the normal pancreas (Figure 1G and Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by sc-RNA-seq data comparing healthy and PDA mouse tissue shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Epithelial cells and fibroblasts only had sporadic Arg1 expression in mouse pancreatic cancer
source: Other cell types, such as epithelial cells and fibroblasts, only had sporadic Arg1 expression.
evidence: This is based on the sc-RNA-seq analysis of mouse pancreatic cancer.

claim: Arg2 was expressed in macrophages at low levels in mouse pancreatic cancer
source: Arg2 was also expressed in macrophages, albeit at low levels, and was the prevalent isoform in tumor-associated granulocytes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by sc-RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Arg2 was the prevalent isoform in tumor-associated granulocytes in mouse pancreatic cancer
source: Arg2 was also expressed in macrophages, albeit at low levels, and was the prevalent isoform in tumor-associated granulocytes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by sc-RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: ARG1 protein was not detected in the healthy pancreas
source: We did not detect ARG1 protein in the healthy pancreas.
evidence: This is based on co-immunofluorescence staining experiments.

claim: Both PanIN and PDA presented with frequent co-localization of the macrophage marker F4/80 with ARG1
source: In contrast, both PanIN and PDA presented with frequent co-localization of the macrophage marker F4/80 with ARG1, consistent with prevalent expression in this cell population (Figure 1H and I and Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunofluorescence staining data shown in Figure 1H and quantified in Figure 1I.

claim: Expression of ARG1 in cell types other than macrophages was rare in mouse pancreatic lesions
source: Consistent with human data, expression of ARG1 in other cell types was rare (Figure 1H and Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: In both mouse and human pancreatic cancer, ARG1 is highly expressed and largely confined to tumors, where it is predominantly expressed in macrophages
source: Thus, both in mouse and human pancreatic cancer, ARG1 is highly expressed and largely confined to tumors, where it is predominantly expressed in macrophages.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the combined data from human and mouse samples presented in Figure 1.

claim: Lyz2Cre/+;Arg1f/f TAMs had none or very low ARG1 protein, indicating efficient Cre recombination
source: ARG1 expression was readily detectable in WT TAMs; in contrast, Lyz2Cre/+;Arg1f/f TAMs had none or very low ARG1 protein, indicating efficient Cre recombination (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Elevated levels of L-Arginine were observed in the Lyz2Cre/+;Arg1f/f TAM medium compared with WT TAM medium
source: We thus performed extracellular metabolomics by liquid chromatography couple tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) and observed elevated levels of L-Arginine in the Lyz2Cre/+;Arg1f/f TAM medium compared with WT TAM medium (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: WT TAMs deplete arginine from their growth medium at an enhanced rate, relative to TAMs lacking Arg1 expression
source: This finding is consistent with WT TAMs depleting arginine from their growth medium at an enhanced rate, relative to TAMs lacking Arg1 expression.
evidence: This represents an inference based on the metabolomics data showing elevated arginine in Arg1-deficient TAM media.

claim: 16 out of 26 KF mice (62%) had invasive disease at 9-16 months of age
source: Accordingly, 16 out of 26 KF mice (62%) had invasive disease; in contrast, only 5 out of 24 KFCA mice had progressed (21%) (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by histopathological evaluation data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Only 5 out of 24 KFCA mice (21%) had invasive disease at 9-16 months of age
source: Accordingly, 16 out of 26 KF mice (62%) had invasive disease; in contrast, only 5 out of 24 KFCA mice had progressed (21%) (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by histopathological evaluation data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: High ARG1 expression was observed in macrophages in KF tissues
source: As expected, we observed high ARG1 expression in macrophages in KF tissues and little to no ARG1 expression in macrophages in KFCA pancreata (Figure 2F).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence staining data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Little to no ARG1 expression was observed in macrophages in KFCA pancreata
source: As expected, we observed high ARG1 expression in macrophages in KF tissues and little to no ARG1 expression in macrophages in KFCA pancreata (Figure 2F).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence staining data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Substantial ARG1 expression was observed in epithelial cells from the KFCA pancreata
source: Surprisingly, we observed substantial ARG1 expression in epithelial cells from the KFCA pancreata, while epithelial cells in KF mice had little to no ARG1 expression (Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence staining data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Epithelial cells in KF mice had little to no ARG1 expression
source: Surprisingly, we observed substantial ARG1 expression in epithelial cells from the KFCA pancreata, while epithelial cells in KF mice had little to no ARG1 expression (Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence staining data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Deletion of Arg1 in myeloid cells impairs malignant progression but unleashes a compensatory upregulation of Arg1 in epithelial cells
source: So, while deletion of Arg1 in myeloid cells impairs malignant progression, it unleashes a compensatory upregulation of Arg1 in epithelial cells.
evidence: This represents a conclusion based on the histopathology and immunofluorescence data.

claim: The epithelia that expressed ARG1 in KFCA mice had an elongated appearance, consistent with tuft cells
source: We noted that the epithelia that expressed ARG1 in KFCA mice had an elongated appearance, consistent with tuft cells, a cell type that is not present in the healthy pancreas but common in low-grade PanINs (Delgiorno et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is based on morphological observations and is supported by citation to Delgiorno et al., 2014 about tuft cells.

claim: Tuft cells are not present in the healthy pancreas but are common in low-grade PanINs
source: We noted that the epithelia that expressed ARG1 in KFCA mice had an elongated appearance, consistent with tuft cells, a cell type that is not present in the healthy pancreas but common in low-grade PanINs (Delgiorno et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Delgiorno et al., 2014.

claim: Tuft cells are the exclusive source of epithelial ARG1 in KFCA samples
source: By co-immunostaining for the tuft cell marker COX1, we confirmed that tuft cells are the exclusive source of epithelial ARG1 in these samples (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A)
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunostaining data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Tuft cell ARG1 expression suggests a tuft cell response to accumulating arginine in the microenvironment
source: By co-immunostaining for the tuft cell marker COX1, we confirmed that tuft cells are the exclusive source of epithelial ARG1 in these samples (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A), suggesting a tuft cell response to accumulating arginine in the microenvironment.
evidence: This represents an inference about the biological significance of tuft cell ARG1 expression.

claim: The percentage of total macrophages was similar between KF and KFCA pancreas
source: The percentage of total macrophages was similar between KF and KFCA pancreas (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D and E, Figure 2—figure supplement 3A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by sc-RNA-seq and immunohistochemistry data shown in the supplementary figures.

claim: Five different macrophage populations were identified based on distinct gene profiles in KF and KFCA pancreata
source: We then subclustered the macrophages, from which we identified five different macrophage populations based on distinct gene profiles (Figure 2H and Figure 2—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by sc-RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 2H.

claim: The macrophage 1 population was defined by Apoe, C1qa, and C1qc markers of TAMs in mouse and human pancreatic cancer
source: The macrophage 1 population was defined by Apoe, C1qa, and C1qc markers of TAMs in mouse and human pancreatic cancer (Kemp et al., 2021a)
evidence: The claim is supported by sc-RNA-seq data and citation to Kemp et al., 2021a.

claim: The macrophage 5 population expressed Ear2 and Retnla
source: while the macrophage 5 population expressed Ear2 and Retnla (Figure 2H).
evidence: The claim is supported by sc-RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Macrophage APOE is tumor promoting
source: Since macrophage APOE (Apolipoprotein E) is tumor promoting (Kemp et al., 2021a)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Kemp et al., 2021a.

claim: A reduction in APOE expression was detected in KFCA compared to KF
source: we performed co-immunofluorescent staining for APOE, F4/80, and ECAD and detected a reduction in APOE expression (Figure 2—figure supplement 3D and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3D and quantified in 3E.

claim: Deletion of Arg1 in myeloid cells led to an upregulation of Arg2 expression, mainly in the macrophage 4 population
source: Intriguingly, sc-RNA-seq revealed that deletion of Arg1 in myeloid cells led to an upregulation of Arg2 expression, mainly in the macrophage 4 population expressing Chil3, Ly6c2, and Clec4e genes (Figure 2I)
evidence: The claim is supported by sc-RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2I.

claim: The upregulation of Arg2 in KFCA macrophages suggests the existence of a compensatory mechanism
source: Intriguingly, sc-RNA-seq revealed that deletion of Arg1 in myeloid cells led to an upregulation of Arg2 expression, mainly in the macrophage 4 population expressing Chil3, Ly6c2, and Clec4e genes (Figure 2I), suggesting the existence of a compensatory mechanism.
evidence: This represents an inference based on the Arg2 upregulation observed in the sc-RNA-seq data.

claim: KFCA macrophages exhibited upregulation of signaling pathways involved in MHC I antigen processing and cross presentation
source: Interestingly, KFCA macrophages, mainly the macrophage 3 population, exhibited upregulation of signaling pathways involved in MHC I antigen processing and cross presentation (Figure 2J and Figure 2—figure supplement 3H)
evidence: The claim is supported by reactome pathway enrichment analysis shown in Figure 2J.

claim: Upregulation of MHC I antigen processing pathways in KFCA macrophages suggests an improvement in antigen-specific CD8+ T cell activation upon Arg1 deletion
source: Interestingly, KFCA macrophages, mainly the macrophage 3 population, exhibited upregulation of signaling pathways involved in MHC I antigen processing and cross presentation (Figure 2J and Figure 2—figure supplement 3H), suggesting an improvement in antigen-specific CD8+ T cell activation upon Arg1 deletion.
evidence: This represents an inference based on the pathway analysis data.

claim: Increased CD8+ T cell infiltration was observed in KFCA pancreata compared to KF
source: As sc-RNA-seq suggested that Arg1 null macrophages have higher antigen presenting activity, we stained KF and KFCA pancreata for CD8 and observed increased CD8+ T cell infiltration in the latter (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: An increase in the percentage of both cytotoxic and exhausted CD8+ T cells was observed in the KFCA model compared with KF
source: From this analysis, we observed an increase in the percentage of both cytotoxic and exhausted CD8+ T cells in the KFCA model compared with KF (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by sc-RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 3D and E.

claim: Expression of genes related to CD8+ T cell cytotoxicity, including Gzmb, Prfn1, and Ifng was upregulated in CD8+ T cells from the KFCA model
source: Correspondingly, expression of genes related to CD8+ T cell cytotoxicity, including Granzyme b (Gzmb), Perforin 1 (Prfn1), and Interferon gamma (Ifng) was upregulated in CD8+ T cells from the KFCA model (Figure 3F).
evidence: The claim is supported by sc-RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: An increase in GZMB-expressing CD8+ T cells was observed in KFCA pancreata
source: Accordingly, co-immunofluorescent staining for CD8, GZMB, and ECAD showed an increase in GZMB-expressing CD8+ T cells in KFCA pancreata (Figure 3G and H).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3G and quantified in Figure 3H.

claim: Expression of genes involved in T cell exhaustion such as Ctla4, Furin, Lag3, and Pdcd1 was upregulated in the KFCA model compared with the KF
source: We also found that the expression of genes involved in T cell exhaustion such as cytotoxic T-lymphocyte associated protein 4 (Ctla4), Furin, lymphocyte activating 3 (Lag3), and programmed cell death 1 (Pdcd1) was upregulated in the KFCA model, compared with the KF (Figure 3I).
evidence: The claim is supported by sc-RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3I.

claim: Deletion of Arg1 in myeloid cells resulted in an increase in CD8+ T cell infiltration and activation, counterbalanced by an increase in exhaustion
source: Taken together, deletion of Arg1 in myeloid cells resulted in an increase in CD8+ T cell infiltration and activation, counterbalanced by an increase in exhaustion as well.
evidence: This represents a summary conclusion based on the CD8+ T cell data presented in Figure 3.

claim: Systemic inhibition of Arginase by CB-1158 increased the infiltration of CD8+ T cells in orthotopic pancreatic tumors
source: Interestingly, we observed that systemic inhibition of Arginase by CB-1158 increased the infiltration of CD8+ T cells (Figure 4B and C), recapitulating our findings from the genetically engineered model.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4B and quantified in Figure 4C.

claim: In the CB-1158 treatment group, GZMB was common in CD8+ T cells, while in the control tissue, GZMB expression was rare
source: While in the control tissue, GZMB expression was rare, in the CB-1158 treatment group, GZMB was common in CD8+ T cells (Figure 4D and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4D and quantified in Figure 4E.

claim: A significant decrease in tumor weight was observed in the combination group of CB-1158 + anti-PD1 compared with the vehicle control group
source: We observed a trending decrease in tumor weight in the CB-1158 + IgG group and a significant decrease in tumor weight in the combination group of CB-1158 + anti-PD1 immune checkpoint blockade compared with our vehicle control group (Figure 4G).
evidence: The claim is supported by tumor weight measurements shown in Figure 4G.

claim: No changes in ARG1 distribution or expression among treatment groups were observed
source: We examined ARG1 expression in macrophages (F4/80+) and epithelial (ECAD+) cells by co-immunofluorescence staining and observed no changes in ARG1 distribution or expression among treatment groups (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The CB-1158 Arginase inhibitor does not affect enzyme production but suppresses its activity
source: We examined ARG1 expression in macrophages (F4/80+) and epithelial (ECAD+) cells by co-immunofluorescence staining and observed no changes in ARG1 distribution or expression among treatment groups (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), consistent with the notion that the CB-1158 Arginase inhibitor does not affect enzyme production but suppresses its activity.
evidence: This represents an inference based on the observation that ARG1 protein levels don't change with CB-1158 treatment.

claim: Large necrotic areas were observed in both CB-1158 and CB-1158 + anti-PD1 groups
source: Hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining showed large necrotic areas in both CB-1158 and CB-1158 + anti-PD1 groups (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by H&E staining shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The combination treatment group showed a significant decrease in cell proliferation compared to the vehicle control group
source: The combination treatment group showed a significant decrease in cell proliferation compared to the vehicle control group (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by Ki67 staining data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and quantified in 1E.

claim: A significant or trending increase in CC3 was observed upon CB-1158 + IgG, vehicle + anti-PD1, or the combination treatment
source: We also observed either a significant or trending increase in CC3 upon CB-1158 + IgG, vehicle + anti-PD1, or the combination treatment (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D and F).
evidence: The claim is supported by cleaved caspase-3 staining data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D and quantified in 1F.

claim: An increase in arginine levels was observed in the tumors from mice treated with CB-1158 and anti-PD1
source: Additionally, metabolomics analysis of these orthotopic tumors revealed an increase in arginine levels in the tumors from mice treated with CB-1158 and anti-PD1 (Figure 4H).
evidence: The claim is supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: Arginine deprivation results in reduced CD8+ T cell proliferation and activation
source: We found that arginine deprivation results in reduced CD8+ T cell proliferation and activation (Figure 4J and K).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro CD8+ T cell assay data shown in Figure 4J and K.

claim: Culturing cells in RPMI media containing urea slightly enhanced CD8+ T cell proliferation and activation, compared to RPMI media control
source: Additionally, we found that culturing cells in RPMI media containing urea sightly enhanced CD8+ T cell proliferation and activation, compared to RPMI media control (Figure 4J and K, gray bars)
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro CD8+ T cell assay data shown in Figure 4J and K.

claim: No enhancement in CD8+ T cell proliferation or activation was observed with ornithine supplementation in complete media
source: Additionally, we found that culturing cells in RPMI media containing urea sightly enhanced CD8+ T cell proliferation and activation, compared to RPMI media control (Figure 4J and K, gray bars), while no enhancement was observed with ornithine supplementation.
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro CD8+ T cell assay data shown in Figure 4J and K.

claim: When cells were cultured in RPMI media lacking arginine, supplementation with ornithine, but not urea, partially rescued the proliferation defect caused by lack of arginine
source: When cells were cultured in RPMI media lacking arginine, supplementation with ornithine, but not urea, partially rescued the proliferation defect caused by lack of arginine.
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro CD8+ T cell assay data shown in Figure 4J and K.

claim: Neither ornithine nor urea rescued the activation defect caused by lack of arginine
source: No further rescue occurred adding urea; neither ornithine nor urea rescued the activation defect caused by lack of arginine.
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro CD8+ T cell assay data shown in Figure 4J and K.

claim: CD8+ T cells require arginine for proliferation and activation
source: We thus concluded that CD8+ T cells require arginine for proliferation and activation, and that the arginine breakdown byproducts are not harmful to CD8+ T cell proliferation nor are they able to fully rescue lack of arginine.
evidence: This represents a conclusion based on the in vitro CD8+ T cell assay data.

claim: The arginine breakdown byproducts are not harmful to CD8+ T cell proliferation
source: We thus concluded that CD8+ T cells require arginine for proliferation and activation, and that the arginine breakdown byproducts are not harmful to CD8+ T cell proliferation nor are they able to fully rescue lack of arginine.
evidence: This represents a conclusion based on the in vitro CD8+ T cell assay data.

claim: The arginine breakdown byproducts are not able to fully rescue lack of arginine for CD8+ T cell function
source: We thus concluded that CD8+ T cells require arginine for proliferation and activation, and that the arginine breakdown byproducts are not harmful to CD8+ T cell proliferation nor are they able to fully rescue lack of arginine.
evidence: This represents a conclusion based on the in vitro CD8+ T cell assay data.

claim: Arginase inhibition in combination with anti-PD1 reduces immune suppression and decreases pancreatic cancer tumor growth
source: Together, these findings indicate that Arginase inhibition in combination with anti-PD1 reduces immune suppression and decreases pancreatic cancer tumor growth (see working model in Figure 5).
evidence: This represents a summary conclusion based on all the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: Abundant myeloid cells in the TME are associated with poor prognosis in multiple types of cancer, including PDA
source: Abundant myeloid cells in the TME are associated with poor prognosis in multiple types of cancer, including PDA (Gentles et al., 2015; Sanford et al., 2013; Tsujikawa et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Gentles et al., 2015; Sanford et al., 2013; and Tsujikawa et al., 2017.

claim: High levels of T cells correlate with longer survival in cancer
source: In contrast, high levels of T cells correlate with longer survival (Gentles et al., 2015; Balachandran et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Gentles et al., 2015 and Balachandran et al., 2017.

claim: Myeloid cells promote pancreatic cancer growth both directly and by inhibiting CD8+ T cell anti-tumor immunity
source: We and others have shown that myeloid cells promote pancreatic cancer growth both directly and by inhibiting CD8+ T cell anti-tumor immunity (Zhang et al., 2017b; Zhang et al., 2017a; Mitchem et al., 2013; Halbrook et al., 2019; Steele et al., 2016; Liou et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations including the authors' own work and others.

claim: Macrophages are plastic cell types, traditionally classified into pro-inflammatory 'M1' and anti-inflammatory 'M2' subtypes, based on their gene expression pattern
source: Macrophages are plastic cell types, traditionally classified into pro-inflammatory 'M1' and anti-inflammatory 'M2' subtypes, based on their gene expression pattern (Mantovani et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Mantovani et al., 2002.

claim: A wealth of evidence now supports the notion that TAMs are distinct from M1 and M2
source: Recently, a wealth of evidence now supports the notion that TAMs are distinct from M1 and M2 (Boyer et al., 2022; DeNardo and Ruffell, 2019; Halbrook et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Boyer et al., 2022; DeNardo and Ruffell, 2019; and Halbrook et al., 2019.

claim: TAMs exhibit heterogeneous populations within an individual tumor
source: Adding further complexity, TAMs also exhibit heterogeneous populations within an individual tumor.
evidence: This represents established knowledge in the field about TAM heterogeneity.

claim: ARG1 is classically considered a 'marker' of the anti-inflammatory M2 state
source: ARG1 is classically considered a 'marker' of the anti-inflammatory M2 state.
evidence: This represents established knowledge in the field about ARG1 as an M2 marker.

claim: Arginases are enzymes that hydrolyze the amino acid L-arginine to urea and L-ornithine in the liver urea cycle
source: Arginases are enzymes that hydrolyze the amino acid L-arginine to urea and L-ornithine in the liver urea cycle (Jenkinson et al., 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Jenkinson et al., 1996.

claim: L-arginine was drastically reduced in the tumor interstitial fluid in an autochthonous PDA mouse model
source: An analysis of plasma metabolites and tumor interstitial fluid in an autochthonous PDA mouse model revealed that L-arginine was drastically reduced in the tumor interstitial fluid (Sullivan et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Sullivan et al., 2019.

claim: Ornithine levels increased in the PDA tumor interstitial fluid compared to plasma
source: Additionally, ornithine levels increased in the PDA tumor interstitial fluid compared to plasma (Sullivan et al., 2019), suggesting arginase contribution to immunosuppression through depletion of arginine.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Sullivan et al., 2019.

claim: The increase in ornithine levels in PDA tumor interstitial fluid suggests arginase contribution to immunosuppression through depletion of arginine
source: Additionally, ornithine levels increased in the PDA tumor interstitial fluid compared to plasma (Sullivan et al., 2019), suggesting arginase contribution to immunosuppression through depletion of arginine.
evidence: This represents an inference based on the metabolite data cited from Sullivan et al., 2019.

claim: There are two isoforms of arginase, ARG1 and ARG2, located in the cytoplasm and mitochondria, respectively
source: There are two isoforms of arginase, ARG1 and ARG2, located in the cytoplasm and mitochondria, respectively (Gotoh et al., 1996; Munder et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Gotoh et al., 1996 and Munder et al., 2005.

claim: The arginase genes share a 58% sequence identity
source: The arginase genes share a 58% sequence identity (Haraguchi et al., 1987) and are almost identical at the catalytic site.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Haraguchi et al., 1987.

claim: The arginase genes are almost identical at the catalytic site
source: The arginase genes share a 58% sequence identity (Haraguchi et al., 1987) and are almost identical at the catalytic site.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Haraguchi et al., 1987.

claim: Arg1 is normally expressed by hepatocytes
source: Arg1 is normally expressed by hepatocytes, but it is also expressed in TAMs in a variety of tumor types.
evidence: This represents established knowledge about Arg1 expression.

claim: Arg2 is located in various cell types, including renal cells, neurons, and macrophages
source: Arg2 is located in various cell types, including renal cells, neurons, and macrophages (Bronte and Zanovello, 2005; Caldwell et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bronte and Zanovello, 2005 and Caldwell et al., 2018.

claim: In a mouse model of Lewis lung carcinoma, myeloid cells express high levels of Arg1, resulting in impaired T cell function
source: In a mouse model of Lewis lung carcinoma, myeloid cells express high levels of Arg1, resulting in impaired T cell function (Rodriguez et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Rodriguez et al., 2004.

claim: Arginase inhibition reduced subcutaneous tumor growth in a dose-dependent manner in a Lewis lung carcinoma model
source: In that study, 3LL tumor cells were implanted subcutaneously in the right flank of the mice, and at the same time, mice were treated with the pan-arginase inhibitor tool compound N-hydroxy-nor-L-Arg. Arginase inhibition reduced subcutaneous tumor growth in a dose-dependent manner.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Rodriguez et al., 2004 (implied from context).

claim: The anti-tumor effect of the arginase inhibitor was in part dependent on T cell function in a Lewis lung carcinoma model
source: The anti-tumor effect of the arginase inhibitor was in part dependent on T cell function, as inhibition on tumor growth was not observed when mice lacking a functional immune system were treated with the arginase inhibitor (Rodriguez et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Rodriguez et al., 2004.

claim: Inhibition of arginase activity by Cpd9 decreased T cell suppression and reduced tumor growth in a KrasG12D lung cancer mouse model
source: In another study (Miret et al., 2019), inhibition of arginase activity by the arginase inhibitor tool compound Cpd9 (Van Zandt et al., 2013) decreased T cell suppression and reduced tumor growth in a KrasG12D lung cancer mouse model.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Miret et al., 2019 and Van Zandt et al., 2013.

claim: In a mouse model of neuroblastoma, myeloid Arg1 expression promoted tumor growth
source: In a more recent study using a mouse model of neuroblastoma, myeloid Arg1 expression promoted tumor growth (Van de Velde et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Van de Velde et al., 2021.

claim: CB-1158 is not cell permeable and thus does not inhibit liver ARG1, which would lead to immediate toxicity
source: CB-1158 is not cell permeable and thus does not inhibit liver ARG1, which would lead to immediate toxicity (Steggerda et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Steggerda et al., 2017.

claim: In vitro, CB-1158 inhibits human recombinant ARG1 and ARG2
source: In vitro, CB-1158 inhibits human recombinant ARG1 and ARG2.
evidence: This represents established knowledge about CB-1158's activity.

claim: The in vivo action of CB-1158 is attributed to inhibition of extracellular ARG1 released by TAMs and other myeloid cells
source: The in vivo action is attributed to inhibition of extracellular ARG1 released by TAMs and other myeloid cells (Steggerda et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Steggerda et al., 2017.

claim: In a model of obesity-driven pancreatic cancer, Arg2 is upregulated in epithelial cells, and its knockdown reduces tumor growth in a cell autonomous manner, independently from immune responses
source: In a model of obesity-driven pancreatic cancer, Arg2 is upregulated in epithelial cells, and its knockdown reduces tumor growth in a cell autonomous manner, independently from immune responses (Zaytouni et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Zaytouni et al., 2017.

claim: Arg2 was not observed in epithelial cells in non-obese KF mice
source: While we did not observe Arg2 expression in epithelial cells in non-obese KF mice, analysis of human data revealed low, but detectable expression of Arg2
evidence: This is based on the sc-RNA-seq data from the study.

claim: Analysis of human data revealed low, but detectable expression of Arg2 in epithelial cells
source: While we did not observe Arg2 expression in epithelial cells in non-obese KF mice, analysis of human data revealed low, but detectable expression of Arg2
evidence: This is based on the sc-RNA-seq analysis of human PDA samples.

claim: In human patients, CB-1158 might work through systemic inhibition of both arginase isoforms in multiple cell compartments, including epithelial cells
source: possibly supporting the possibility that, in human patients, CB-1158 might work through systemic inhibition of both arginase isoforms in multiple cell compartments, including epithelial cells.
evidence: This represents speculation about the mechanism of action of CB-1158 in human patients.

claim: One of the mechanisms by which myeloid cells promote immune suppression and tumor growth in pancreatic cancer is through overexpression and activity of Arg1
source: Our findings show that one of the mechanisms by which myeloid cells promote immune suppression and tumor growth in pancreatic cancer is through overexpression and activity of Arg1.
evidence: This represents a key conclusion of the study based on all the experimental data.

claim: Arginase inhibition may be an effective therapeutic strategy to enhance anti-tumor immune responses
source: Thus, arginase inhibition may be an effective therapeutic strategy to enhance anti-tumor immune responses.
evidence: This represents a conclusion and therapeutic implication based on the study's findings.

claim: Arg1 drives immune suppression in pancreatic cancer by depleting arginine and inhibiting T cell activation
source: Our data demonstrate that Arg1 drives immune suppression in pancreatic cancer by depleting arginine and inhibiting T cell activation.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the abstract, supported by all the experimental data in the study.

claim: CB-1158 is currently evaluated as a single agent and in combination with immune checkpoint therapy or chemotherapy in patients with solid tumors
source: CB-1158 is currently evaluated as a single agent and in combination with immune checkpoint therapy or chemotherapy in patients with solid tumors (https://www.clinicaltrials.gov/, NCT02903914 and NCT03314935).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to clinical trial registrations.
